title: Approve an agent action from a CLI
description: Start a durable agent run from TypeScript, see the exact tool call it wants to make, and approve or reject it before it happens. The agent only sends you a Slack DM.
prerequisites: A Glean instance with durable agent runs available
Permission to create agents in Agent Builder
The **Slack Actions** tool pack available in Agent Builder, and your Slack account connected in Glean, so the agent can send you a direct message
Permission to sign in with the `agents` scope

questions.prompt: What is your work email? It finds your Glean instance and signs you in.
After you save the agent in Agent Builder, what is its agent ID (the 32-character ID after /agents/ in its URL)?

verification.expectedDuration: about 2 minutes; approve one run and reject another, and check Slack

codeAssets.description: A TypeScript CLI that starts a durable run, shows the pending tool call, and sends your decision, with offline tests

steps.title: Install and run the offline tests
steps.command:
cd human-in-the-loop-agent && npm ci
npm test
steps.description: Run every later command from this directory in the same shell. The tests run the real SDK against local HTTP handlers; they don't sign in or contact Glean or Slack.

steps.title: Create the agent and paste its instructions
steps.description: In Glean, open **Agents** from the left navigation and click **Create agent**. **Auto mode** is selected by default, and **Builder Assistant** opens beside the agent; you don't need it (if it asks you to describe the agent first, paste these instructions into it). Click the name at the top of the builder and rename it `Cookbook approval demo`. Replace any text under **Instructions** with the text this command prints.

steps.title: Add the Slack tool
steps.description: In the **Capabilities** tab, under **Tools**, search for **Slack Actions** and add it. Under **Write tools**, keep only **Send Slack message to user**. Leave **Allow agent to use write tools without approval** unchecked: that checkbox is the approval boundary this recipe demonstrates. A spec file can't set this up for you, because it refers to Slack by a tool provider ID that is different on every Glean instance.

steps.title: Set the trigger and publish
steps.description: In the **Triggers** tab, set **When should the agent run?** to **Manually run** and **What type of input does it need?** to **Chat message**. Click **Publish**. Until you publish, your edits are only a draft, and API runs use the published agent.

steps.title: Copy the agent ID
steps.description: Click **Share** at the top right of the agent. Under **Publishing options**, the **API** section shows the **Agent ID** with a copy button; use it as `<agent-id>` below. You don't need **Create token** there: the next step signs you in instead. The ID is also the 32-character value after `/agents/` in the page URL.

steps.title: Sign in
steps.description: Complete browser sign-in yourself. `glean-auth` finds your Glean backend from your email and keeps a refreshable session outside this project, so a run can wait for you. If OAuth isn't available, copy `.env.example` to `.env` and set `GLEAN_API_TOKEN` to a user-scoped token with the `agents` scope instead. Never paste a token into a chat or a command.

steps.title: Run the agent and decide
steps.description: The command starts one durable run, waits for the agent to pause, and shows the tool, what it does, and its exact arguments. Type `a` to approve that one call (the DM arrives), `r` to reject it (nothing is sent), `c` to cancel the run, or press **Enter** to leave it waiting. If the run finishes without asking, the Slack tool isn't added, **Allow agent to use write tools without approval** is checked, or the agent wasn't published.

steps.title: Follow the API calls
steps.description: `--show-json` prints each API request and response body under the SDK call that sent it, so you can follow `run_id` and `interaction_id` from one call to the next. Leave it off to see only the review. The JSON includes the tool arguments, so keep it out of shared logs.

steps.title: Pick a waiting run back up
steps.description: Closing the CLI or reaching the 120-second wait doesn't cancel the run; the CLI prints the full resume command, with the agent and run IDs. After a decision, a resumed run can take a few minutes to finish; if the wait runs out, resume again. Without a terminal to ask in, resume prints a decision command bound to the pending interaction ID; run it only after a person has reviewed that call.

steps.title: Check approve, reject, and cancel
steps.description: Approve one run and confirm exactly one DM arrives. Run the command again and reject; confirm no DM arrives and the agent says the message was not sent. Run it a third time, press **Enter**, then run the resume command it printed and cancel the run (`c`); it ends cancelled with nothing pending. Only Slack can show whether a message was sent.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.description: Delete or archive the `Cookbook approval demo` agent in Agent Builder when you're done. Nothing here deletes runs, messages, or agents.

demoQueries.query: Start a run and approve the Slack DM it asks to send.
demoQueries.expectedBehavior: The run pauses in REQUIRES_INPUT with one TOOL_APPROVAL for Send Slack message to user, showing the message text, and nothing arrives in Slack yet. After approval the same run reaches SUCCEEDED and exactly one DM arrives.

demoQueries.query: Start a run and reject the Slack DM it asks to send.
demoQueries.expectedBehavior: The run pauses before sending. After rejection the same run reaches SUCCEEDED, the agent replies that the message was not sent, and no DM arrives.

demoQueries.query: Start a run, leave it waiting, then resume it and cancel.
demoQueries.expectedBehavior: Leaving the prompt sends nothing and keeps the run in REQUIRES_INPUT. Resuming shows the same pending call; cancelling ends the run CANCELLED with no pending interactions and no DM.

apiFlow.intro: An approval takes four calls, and each one needs a value from an earlier response. Keep the `run_id` from the start, poll until the run needs a decision, and answer with the `interaction_id` the person reviewed. These are the bodies from one approved run, with example IDs and empty messages left out.

inputs.description: The published agent's ID: the 32-character ID after /agents/ in its Agent Builder URL.
APPROVE or REJECT, chosen by the person who reviewed the tool call.

calls.title: Start a durable run
calls.description: Send the message for the agent. The response is the new run, still working.

highlights.note: DURABLE keeps the run on the server, so it can stop and wait for a person.
false returns the run as one JSON body instead of a stream.
Keep this. Every later call names the run by it.

calls.title: Poll until the run needs a decision
calls.description: Get the run every 2 seconds while its state is QUEUED or RUNNING. REQUIRES_INPUT means the agent stopped before a tool that needs approval.

highlights.note: Stop polling here. The run waits for a decision; it doesn't time out while it waits.
Identifies this exact tool call. The decision must name it.
Show the person display_name, description, and these exact arguments. A decision can't change them.

calls.title: Send the person's decision
calls.description: Answer the call the person reviewed. To stop instead, send the same run_id to POST /api/agents/{agent_id}/cancellations.

highlights.note: The run ID goes in the body here, not the path.
Use the ID the person reviewed, never a newly polled one.
The same run continues. The tool runs only if the decision was APPROVE.

calls.title: Poll until the run ends
calls.description: Keep getting the run until it reaches SUCCEEDED, FAILED, CANCELLED, or EXPIRED. If it pauses again, that's a new tool call to review.

highlights.note: The agent's reply is the last text part in output.messages. A real run can also return messages with empty content.

aiPrompt: Copy the scaffold and follow its numbered steps in one shell session. Guide the user through creating and publishing the agent in Agent Builder with the supplied instructions and the Slack Actions tool Send Slack message to user, with Allow agent to use write tools without approval unchecked, then ask for the agent ID. Do not create the agent from a spec file. Use the shipped npm run login and npm start commands; do not recreate authentication. When the CLI shows a pending tool call, show the user the tool and exact arguments and ask them to decide. Never run a --decision command, approve, reject, or cancel without the user choosing it for that exact interaction ID. Starting the recipe is not permission to approve. Run the offline tests without credentials; only Slack can confirm whether a message was sent.
llmContext: Uses @gleanwork/api-client 0.20.15 with an @gleanwork/auth createGleanTokenProvider session for the agents scope (GLEAN_API_TOKEN only as a fallback). createRun with execution_mode: DURABLE and stream: false; getRun polls; respondToRun and cancelRun post to /api/agents/{agent_id}/responses and /api/agents/{agent_id}/cancellations with run_id in the body. A pending approval has interaction_id, type TOOL_APPROVAL, display_name, description, tool_id, and arguments. Decisions are APPROVE or REJECT for the reviewed interaction_id only and cannot edit arguments. The client never retries automatically, because a retried start creates a second run. resume, status, and cancel take --agent-id and --run-id. Agent spec files refer to built-in tools such as Slack by a per-instance toolProviderId, so this recipe has the user create the agent in Agent Builder instead of importing a spec.

content.problem: A tool can change something outside Glean before anyone has a chance to review it. A durable agent run stops when the agent reaches a tool that needs confirmation, stores the exact call, and waits. Your application reads the call, shows it to a person, and sends their decision; the same run then continues. This recipe walks that flow with a small TypeScript CLI and an agent whose only tool sends you a Slack DM.

guardrails.title: Keep the approval boundary on the tool
guardrails.rule: Leave Allow agent to use write tools without approval unchecked for the tool you want reviewed. Asking for consent in the agent instructions is not an approval gate. If a run finishes without pausing, treat it as a configuration error.

guardrails.title: Decide on the call you showed
guardrails.rule: Send the interaction ID the person reviewed, never a newly polled one. One decision covers one call: if the agent pauses again, show the new call. A decision cannot edit arguments; reject and start again instead.

guardrails.title: Never approve without a person
guardrails.rule: Nothing in this recipe approves automatically. Without a terminal to ask in, the CLI prints a decision command bound to the pending interaction ID; a coding assistant must still ask the user before running it. Only count input given after the call is on screen: the CLI throws away anything typed while it waited, so a keypress made earlier cannot approve a call nobody has seen.

guardrails.title: Don't retry a start
guardrails.rule: Retrying a start after an unknown outcome creates a second run, so the client never retries on its own. After a network error, read the run before doing anything else. Keep credentials and printed tool arguments out of shared logs.

limitations.title: One pending call at a time
limitations.description: The CLI reviews a single tool approval and refuses a run waiting on more than one. Multi-call approval batches are outside this recipe.

limitations.title: The agent is built by hand
limitations.description: Agent spec files refer to built-in tools such as Slack by a tool provider ID that differs on every Glean instance, and an unresolved tool is dropped without an error. Until that's portable, creating the agent in Agent Builder is the reliable path.

limitations.title: Durable is not crash recovery
limitations.description: A run survives your connection closing, not a server worker crashing. An active turn times out after 30 minutes; runs waiting for approval don't expire through that timeout.

limitations.title: Cancelling is not undo
limitations.description: Cancellation stops future work. A tool call that already ran stays done, and closing the CLI never cancels a run.

takeItFurther: Replace the terminal prompt with an approval screen in your application. Keep the reviewed interaction ID and arguments attached to the decision.
Swap in another write tool once you have confirmed it requires confirmation. Show large numeric arguments from the raw response, since JSON.parse rounds integers above 2^53.
